lessons.title: Math is Boundless
lessons.objective: I can create and describe geometric designs using repetition, patterns, and rhythm, and use a pattern unit to predict what comes next.
lessons.languageObjective: I can describe a design using the words repetition, pattern, pattern unit, and rhythm.

concept.heading: Repetition, pattern, and rhythm
concept.intro: The first element of design is repetition: the same object or shape repeated multiple times. Because it involves one object, it has predictability. The second element is a pattern: a set of objects or shapes repeated and arranged in a regular order.
concept.keyIdea: Tessellations, Geometry & Mathematical Art. 1. Tessellation: Repeating pattern of polygons covering a plane with zero gaps and no overlaps. 2. Interior angles around every vertex must sum to exactly 360°. 3. Use translations, rotations, and reflections to generate symmetrical tile patterns

worked.title: Watch me use a pattern unit
lines: A border repeats: pink circle, purple square, blue triangle, pink circle, purple square, blue triangle, ...
The pattern unit is 3 shapes long: circle, square, triangle.
To predict shape number 12, I divide: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 with no remainder, so shape 12 ends a complete unit — it is the blue triangle.
The next three shapes after any complete unit will be a pink circle, a purple square, and a blue triangle.
linesEs: Un borde se repite: círculo rosa, cuadrado morado, triángulo azul, círculo rosa, cuadrado morado, triángulo azul, …
La unidad del patrón mide 3 figuras: círculo, cuadrado, triángulo.
Para predecir la figura número 12, divido: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 sin residuo, así que la figura 12 termina una unidad completa — es el triángulo azul.
Las tres figuras que siguen después de cualquier unidad completa serán un círculo rosa, un cuadrado morado y un triángulo azul.
worked.titleEs: Mírame usar una unidad de patrón

together.title: Let's predict shape number 20 together
lines: The pattern unit is still 3 shapes long.
20 ÷ 3 = 6 complete units with a remainder of 2, because 6 × 3 = 18 and 20 − 18 = 2.
A remainder of 2 means shape 20 is the second shape in the unit.
The second shape is the purple square.
linesEs: La unidad del patrón sigue midiendo 3 figuras.
20 ÷ 3 = 6 unidades completas con residuo de 2, porque 6 × 3 = 18 y 20 − 18 = 2.
Un residuo de 2 significa que la figura 20 es la segunda figura de la unidad.
La segunda figura es el cuadrado morado.

vocabulary.definition: The same object, shape, or form repeated multiple times.
vocabulary.example: The same tile, over and over, all the way along the border.

vocabulary.definition: A set of objects or shapes that are repeated and arranged in a regular order.
vocabulary.example: Circle, square, triangle, circle, square, triangle …

vocabulary.definition: The smallest chunk of a pattern that repeats.
vocabulary.example: circle · square · triangle — the chunk that starts over.

vocabulary.definition: A design element created by varying the placement, size, orientation, or order of the same objects or shapes.
vocabulary.example: The same circles, but sizes and spacing change as your eye travels.

vocabulary.definition: Being able to know what comes next because the design follows a rule.
vocabulary.example: Shape 25 must be a circle — the unit repeats every 3.

lessons.title: Math is Mine
lessons.objective: I can look back at my answers from Lesson 1-1, describe how my math biography has changed this year, and recognize ways we are all doers of math.
lessons.languageObjective: I can compare my beginning-of-year and end-of-year math stories using the words then, now, changed, and grown.

concept.heading: Your math story, one year later
concept.intro: In Lesson 1-1 you estimated riders on a Ferris wheel, decomposed 78.5, and wrote your math story. The question now is not 'what is math?' but 'how have I changed as a doer of math?'
concept.keyIdea: Mathematical Reflection & Portfolio Culmination. 1. Synthesize grade-level mastery across Number Systems, Ratios, Expressions, Geometry, and Statistics. 2. Justify problem-solving strategies using multiple representations (equations, graphs, models). 3. Reflect on mathematical growth and communicate solutions with precision and confidence

worked.title: Watch me reread my September work
lines: In September I estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4 = 80 riders — 'about 80.'
Now I can go further with this year's math: at 6 turns an hour, that wheel moves about 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour.
Same wheel, same me — but my toolbox grew. That difference IS my math story.
linesEs: En septiembre estimé la rueda de la fortuna: 20 cabinas con unas 4 personas cada una son 20 × 4 = 80 personas — «unas 80».
Ahora puedo ir más lejos con las matemáticas de este año: a 6 vueltas por hora, esa rueda mueve unas 80 × 6 = 480 personas por hora.
La misma rueda, el mismo yo — pero mi caja de herramientas creció. Esa diferencia es mi historia matemática.
worked.titleEs: Mírame releer mi trabajo de septiembre

together.title: Let's revisit 78.5 with this year's tools
lines: In September we decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5 and 80 − 1.5.
This year we learned new ways to say the same number: 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2.
Find one more way to write 78.5 using something you learned this year.
linesEs: Este año aprendimos maneras nuevas de decir el mismo número: 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2.
Halla una manera más de escribir 78.5 usando algo que hayas aprendido este año.
together.titleEs: Volvamos a 78.5 con las herramientas de este año

vocabulary.definition: The story of your relationship with math — and how it has changed over time.
vocabulary.example: September: “I am not a math person.” June: “I can explain why it works.”

vocabulary.definition: To look back at what you did, felt, and learned, and think about what it means.
vocabulary.example: Looking back at the tram problem: what worked, what you would change.

vocabulary.definition: The change between what you could do before and what you can do now.
vocabulary.example: In Unit 1 you estimated 80 riders; now you find 480 riders per hour.

vocabulary.definition: Trusting yourself to try a problem, even when the first attempt might fail.
vocabulary.example: Starting a hard problem before you are sure it will work.

vocabulary.definition: The people and places around you — where math shows up outside the classroom.
vocabulary.example: The people and places where math shows up — home, work, the neighborhood.

title: My Math, Next
mission: Explore a pattern beyond the first few cases and tell the story of your mathematical growth. Make a claim, test it, and name your next question.
investigate: Use the first few stages to predict stage 20.
Write a rule that can describe any stage. What does that let you do?
Find two different strategies and explain when each is useful.
create: Build a mini-exhibit of a pattern and your thinking. Include an early attempt, a revision, a general rule, and one question you would like to investigate next.

support.prompt: In geometric design, what is repetition?
choices: A set of different shapes arranged randomly
Shapes that vary in size and order of appearance
The same object or shape repeated multiple times
support.explanation: Repetition involves one repeated object, shape, or form — and because of that, it has predictability.
feedback: A random arrangement has no rule, so it is neither repetition nor a pattern.
Varying size and order describes rhythm, not repetition.
Color alone does not make a design element — repetition is about a repeated shape.
hints: The word itself is a clue: something repeats.
How many different objects does repetition involve?
One object or shape, repeated multiple times.

support.prompt: A border shows: pink circle, purple square, blue triangle, pink circle, purple square, blue triangle. What are the next three shapes?
choices: Blue triangle, purple square, pink circle
Pink circle, purple square, blue triangle
Pink circle, blue triangle, purple square
support.explanation: The pattern unit is circle, square, triangle, so it repeats in the same order: a pink circle, a purple square, and a blue triangle.
feedback: That reverses the unit — a pattern repeats in the SAME order, not backwards.
That swaps the square and triangle; the unit's order never changes.
A pattern has predictability — that is exactly what makes it a pattern.
hints: Find the chunk that repeats.
The unit is circle, square, triangle.
After a triangle, the unit starts over.

support.prompt: In the circle-square-triangle border, how many shapes long is the pattern unit?
support.explanation: The smallest repeating chunk is circle, square, triangle — 3 shapes.
feedback: 1 shape would be repetition of a single object, but here three different shapes repeat.
After 2 shapes (circle, square) the pattern has not started over yet — the triangle is part of the unit.
6 shapes is two copies of the unit — the pattern unit is the SMALLEST chunk that repeats.
hints: Where does the pattern start over?
List the shapes until you see the first shape again.
Circle, square, triangle — then it restarts.

support.prompt: What is rhythm in geometric design?
choices: The same objects or shapes with varying placement, size, or order of appearance
One shape repeated exactly, over and over
Shapes arranged in a strict, predictable order
A design with no shapes at all
support.explanation: Rhythm is created by varying the placement and order of appearance of the same objects or shapes — it gives patterns a flow and often lacks predictability.
feedback: One shape repeated exactly is repetition, not rhythm.
A strict predictable order describes a pattern; rhythm varies.
Rhythm still uses objects and shapes — it varies how they appear.
hints: Rhythm uses the SAME shapes as a pattern might.
What is different is how they appear.
Their size, placement, and order VARY.

support.prompt: Where have you seen geometric patterns decorating a building, clothing, or artwork? Describe the design.
support.frame: I have seen a geometric pattern on ___ .
support.explanation: The floor of our school hallway has a pattern: two gray tiles, then one blue tile, repeated down the whole hall. The pattern unit is 3 tiles, so I can always predict the next tile.

support.prompt: In Lesson 1-1 you estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars each holding about 4 people. About how many riders was that?
support.explanation: 20 × 4 = 80 — the same estimate you made in September, and it still holds up.
feedback: That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 20 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: This is the very first estimate of the year — 20 groups of 4.
Multiply the cars by the riders per car.

support.prompt: In September you decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5. Which of these ALSO equals 78.5, using division?
support.explanation: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, so it is another way to write the same number from Lesson 1-1.
feedback: 78.5 ÷ 2 = 39.25 — that halves the number instead of rebuilding it.
156 ÷ 2 = 78, which drops the 0.5.
hints: Which quotient lands exactly on 78.5?
Try doubling 78.5 first.
Double 78.5 first. The number you land on is the one being divided by 2.

support.prompt: Which statement matches this lesson's big idea about math stories?
choices: Our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow
Your math story was finished when you wrote it in September
Only students with high grades have a math story
A math story never changes once it is written
support.explanation: The summary says it directly: we are all doers of math, and our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow and advance.
feedback: September was the BEGINNING of this year's story — today's lesson exists because the story kept going.
Everyone has a math story; being a doer of math is not about grades.
The whole point of comparing September to June is that the story DID change.
hints: Why are you rereading Lesson 1-1 today?
Because something changed between then and now.
Stories grow and evolve — which option says that?

support.prompt: How has your attitude about math changed over the year?
support.frame: In September I thought math was ___ .
support.explanation: In September I thought being good at math meant being fast. Now I think it means sticking with a problem — some of my best work this year came on the second or third try.

support.prompt: Predict the output for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: y = 4x + 1; when x = 5, y = 21. At x = 0, y = 1. Every increase of 1 in x adds 4 to y.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: A pattern starts with 1 fixed units and adds 4 units for every step. How many units are at step 6?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: The same pattern follows y = 4x + 1. At what input x is y = 37?
support.explanation: Subtract the fixed 1, then divide by 4: (37 − 1) ÷ 4 = 9.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The pattern unit circle-square-triangle repeats. What is shape number 12?
core.explanation: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 with no remainder, so shape 12 ends a complete unit — the triangle, which is the last shape of the unit.
feedback: The circle is position 1 of a unit — that would need a remainder of 1, but 12 ÷ 3 has remainder 0.
The square is position 2 of a unit — that would need a remainder of 2, but 12 ÷ 3 has remainder 0.
It CAN be determined — a pattern's predictability is the point of the pattern unit.
hints: The unit is 3 shapes long. Divide 12 by 3.
12 ÷ 3 = 4 exactly, remainder 0.
No remainder means the LAST shape of the unit.

core.prompt: Same pattern. What is shape number 20?
choices: The 20th shape starts a new pattern
core.explanation: 20 ÷ 3 = 6 remainder 2 (since 6 × 3 = 18 and 20 − 18 = 2), and the second shape in the unit is the purple square.
feedback: The circle needs a remainder of 1, but 20 − 18 = 2.
The triangle needs a remainder of 0, but 20 ÷ 3 leaves a remainder of 2.
The pattern never changes its unit — position 20 is still inside the same repeating pattern.
hints: How many complete units of 3 fit in 20?
6 units use 18 shapes; 20 − 18 = 2 left over.
Count 2 into the unit: circle, then ___ .

core.prompt: How many COMPLETE pattern units appear in the first 18 shapes of the circle-square-triangle border?
core.explanation: Each unit is 3 shapes, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6 complete units.
feedback: 3 is the size of one unit, not the number of units in 18 shapes.
That divides 18 by 2, but the unit has 3 shapes, not 2.
That subtracts 18 − 3 instead of dividing.
hints: One unit uses 3 shapes.
How many groups of 3 are in 18?
Divide 18 by 3.

core.prompt: How is a design with rhythm different from a pattern?
choices: Rhythm uses shapes and a pattern does not
A pattern varies its shapes and rhythm never does
There is no difference between them
Rhythm varies size, orientation, and order, so it often lacks predictability; a pattern repeats in a regular order
core.explanation: A pattern repeats its unit in a regular arrangement, so it is predictable. Rhythm keeps the same objects but varies how they appear, giving flow without predictability.
feedback: Both use objects and shapes — the difference is in how they are arranged.
That is backwards: the PATTERN is the regular, predictable one, and rhythm is the one that varies.
They differ in exactly one important way: predictability.
hints: Think about predicting the next shape in each.
In which one can you always predict it?
A pattern is predictable; rhythm often is not.

core.prompt: A painting shows circles whose colors, sizes, and thickness vary, along with the number of concentric circles inside each one. Describe how the painting demonstrates rhythm.
core.frame: The painting uses the same object, but varies ___ .
core.explanation: The painting demonstrates rhythm because it uses the same object — a circle — but everything about how the circles appear varies: their colors, their sizes, their thickness, and how many rings sit inside each one. There is a flow, but no repeating unit you could use to predict the next circle.

core.prompt: Now stretch the September estimate with this year's math: about 80 riders per turn, 6 turns each hour. About how many riders per hour?
core.explanation: 80 riders on each of 6 turns is 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour — a rate, one of this year's tools.
feedback: That divides 80 by 6 instead of multiplying.
That adds 80 + 6 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 6.
hints: Each turn carries a full load of about 80.
There are 6 turns in an hour.

core.prompt: Percents were new this year. What is 50% of 157?
core.explanation: 50% means half, and 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — the very number you decomposed back in Lesson 1-1.
feedback: 77.5 is half of 155, not 157.
107 subtracts 50 from 157 instead of taking 50 percent.
hints: 50% of a number is half of it.
Half of 157 means 157 ÷ 2.
Check your answer by doubling it — you should land back on 157.

core.prompt: Which of these is the strongest evidence that YOUR math reasoning grew this year?
choices: You finish worksheets faster than in September
You memorized more answers than before
You can explain why a method works, not just follow its steps
core.explanation: Constructing and explaining reasoning is the growth this lesson asks you to look for — it is what makes the math yours.
feedback: Speed can grow without understanding growing — it is not evidence of reasoning.
Memorized answers work only on problems you have already seen; reasoning works on new ones.
Nobody stopped making mistakes — growth shows in how you respond to them.
hints: Think about reasoning, not speed or memory.
Which option is about understanding WHY?
Explaining why a method works shows the math is yours.

core.prompt: What challenges did you face in math this year, and how did you respond to these challenges?
core.frame: My biggest challenge this year was ___ .
core.explanation: Dividing fractions was my biggest challenge — my first quiz did not go well. I responded by drawing models before using the rule, and by asking my partner to explain her way. By the next unit I could explain WHY dividing by one-half doubles a number.

core.prompt: Predict the output for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: y = 5x + 1; when x = 5, y = 26. At x = 0, y = 1. Every increase of 1 in x adds 5 to y.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

core.prompt: A pattern starts with 1 fixed units and adds 4 units for every step. How many units are at step 6?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The same pattern follows y = 4x + 1. At what input x is y = 37?
core.explanation: Subtract the fixed 1, then divide by 4: (37 − 1) ÷ 4 = 9.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

stretch.prompt: The circle-square-triangle pattern continues. What is shape number 25?
stretch.explanation: 25 ÷ 3 = 8 remainder 1 (since 8 × 3 = 24 and 25 − 24 = 1), and the first shape of the unit is the pink circle.
feedback: The square needs a remainder of 2, but 25 − 24 = 1.
The triangle needs a remainder of 0, but 25 ÷ 3 leaves a remainder of 1.
A pattern is boundless — it continues, so shape 25 exists and is predictable.
hints: How many complete units of 3 fit in 25?
8 units use 24 shapes; 25 − 24 = 1 left over.
A remainder of 1 means the FIRST shape of the unit.

stretch.prompt: Which element of geometric design often LACKS predictability?
stretch.explanation: Rhythm varies the size, orientation, and order of appearance of the same objects, so it gives flow but often lacks predictability.
feedback: Repetition is the MOST predictable element — one shape repeats exactly.
A pattern repeats its unit in a regular order, which is what makes it predictable.
The pattern unit is the source of a pattern's predictability, not something that lacks it.
hints: Which element varies size, orientation, and order?
Repetition and patterns both follow strict rules.
The one that varies is the unpredictable one.

stretch.prompt: Create a design that has repetition, pattern, AND rhythm. Describe (or sketch) it, and label where each element appears.
stretch.explanation: My design is a picture frame. The outer border is repetition: one gold square repeated all the way around. The inner border is a pattern: star, moon, star, moon in a regular order, so its pattern unit is 2 shapes. The center has rhythm: the same star shape scattered across the middle in different sizes, angles, and colors, so it flows but cannot be predicted.

stretch.prompt: Which set shows THREE correct ways to write 78.5 using skills from this year?
stretch.explanation: All three rebuild 78.5 exactly: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, 50% of 157 = 78.5, and 78½ = 78.5.
feedback: 156 ÷ 2 = 78, so that set contains an error.
78¼ = 78.25, so that set contains an error.
25% of 157 = 39.25, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check every member of each set against 78.5.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all three land exactly on 78.5.

stretch.prompt: How have your math thinking HABITS changed from the beginning of the year to now? (Not what you know — how you think.)
stretch.frame: My old habit was ___ ; my new habit is ___ .
stretch.explanation: In September my habit was to answer fast and move on. Now my habits are to estimate first so I can judge my answer, to try a second strategy when the first stalls, and to ask 'does this make sense?' before calling anything done. The facts I learned may fade, but I think these habits will stay.
